I,	The Constitution of India establishes a federal structure with a pronounced unitary bias.
Legislative authority is distributed between the Union and the States through three lists in the
Seventh Schedule - the Union List, the State List, and the Concurrent List. Parliament exercises
exclusive authority over subjects in the Union List, including defence, foreign affairs, and atomic
energy. States may legislate on State List subjects such as police, public health, and agriculture.
On Concurrent List subjects, both Parliament and State Legislatures may legislate; however, in
case of conflict, Union law prevails by virtue of the doctrine of repugnancy under Article 254.
The Supreme Court in State of West Bengal v. Union of India affirmed that India is not a league of
sovereign States but a union from which no unit may secede. This centralising vision is further
reflected in Article 356, which empowers the President to assume governance of a State when
constitutional machinery breaks down. Critics argue that such provisions reduce States to
administrative appendages of the Centre, diluting the essence of federalism. Proponents contend,
however, that strong central authority is indispensable in a vast, diverse democracy, particularly
for preserving national integrity and coordinating responses to economic and security crises.
The Indian model has therefore been characterised by scholars as a "quasi-federal" arrangement -
federal in form but unitary in spirit. The balance between central authority and State autonomy
continues to be tested in contemporary political disputes, particularly over subjects like taxation,
law enforcement, and environmental regulation, where the jurisdictional lines are frequently
contested in constitutional litigation before the Supreme Court.

I.	The authority of courts in a constitutional democracy rests not on coercive power alone but on the
legitimacy conferred by the rule of law. The doctrine of contempt of court is one of the most visible
expressions of this authority. Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, contempt is classified as
civil contempt - wilful disobedience of a court order - and criminal contempt, which includes
publication of material that scandalises or tends to lower the authority of any court.
The Supreme Court has consistently held that contempt jurisdiction must be exercised with great
caution, and only when there is a clear and present danger to the administration of justice. In Re:
Arundhati Roy, the Court reiterated that freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) does not
immunise individuals from liability for statements that substantially interfere with judicial

IV.	The very notion that the maximum welfare of all could be achieved by a system in which each
individual seeks to maximize their own individual self-interest regardless of its impact on others is
about as rational as the assumption of efficient market theory that each individual makes rational
decisions in pursuit of their own economic self-interest. The constitutional constraints imposed on
individual freedom by protection for the rights of other individuals and for the rights of the
collective are distorted by polarizing populism into a competitive battle to see whose claim to
rights will gain a temporary upper hand. But the selfishness of all may be no more rational or
virtuous than the selfishness of a single monarch or autocrat, especially when that all is merely
the all of a single class, community, race, religious group, nation or group of nations. It is simply
more balanced and constrained in its expression by countervailing forces. Is this really the best we
can do? Many of the problems associated with the practice of democracy have arisen from a
misconception of what it actually is. As Francis Fukuyama reminds us, modern democracy evolved
in combination with two other social institutions-the nation state and rule of law, the capacity to
preserve secure national boundaries and the capacity to regulate activities within those
boundaries according to impersonal principles and administrative processes. Democracy flourished
in the past only under conditions where populations were able to exercise the freedom for self-
determinism and the effective power for self-governance. Efforts to introduce or impose democratic
forms of government on populations which had not yet developed the capacity for self-defense, self-
governance and rule of law have always been doomed to failure or a very long period of gestation
until these two other conditions could be met.

appropriate response.
The Concept of Law by H.L.A. Hart
Law's Empire by Ronald Dworkin
The Morality of Law by Lon L. Fuller
In The Concept of Law, H.L.A. Hart advances a positivist account of law grounded in social
practice rather than natural morality. Hart distinguishes between primary rules, which impose
obligations directly on individuals, and secondary rules, which confer powers on officials to create,
modify, and adjudicate law. Central to his theory is the "rule of recognition" - a master criterion by
which valid laws are identified within a legal system. Hart maintains that law and morality are
conceptually separate: a law need not be morally good to be legally valid. He concedes, however,
that legal rules carry an "open texture," meaning that language is inherently indeterminate at its
edges, and judges must inevitably exercise discretion when rules fail to govern unforeseen
situations with certainty. For Hart, the task of legal theory is descriptive - to analyze law as a
social institution shaped by human convention rather than divine command or universal moral
principle.
Ronald Dworkin's Law's Empire challenges Hart's positivist framework by arguing that law
cannot be understood apart from its moral dimensions. Dworkin contends that law is not merely a
collection of social facts but an interpretive enterprise in which judges must construct the "best
moral reading" of existing legal materials. He introduces the metaphor of the "chain novel," where
each judge adds a new chapter that must cohere with prior decisions while simultaneously
advancing justice and moral integrity. Dworkin rejects the notion of judicial discretion in hard
cases, insisting that there is always a right answer derivable from the moral principles embedded
within a legal system. His theory of "law as integrity" holds that judges must interpret rules
consistently with the moral commitments that best justify the community's legal practices. For
Dworkin, law is fundamentally a political and moral achievement, not a neutral social artifact.
Lon Fuller's The Morality of Law occupies a distinctive position by arguing that law carries an
inherent "inner morality" rooted in procedural demands. Fuller identifies eight requirements - the
"eight desiderata" - that any genuine legal order must satisfy: laws must be general, publicly
promulgated, prospective, clear, non-contradictory, practicable, stable over time, and administered
consistently. He terms this the "morality of aspiration," a standard against which legal systems
may succeed or fail in governing citizens with fairness and predictability. Fuller criticises
positivism for ignoring this internal morality, arguing that a system which systematically violates
these requirements degenerates into something that cannot properly be called law at all. Unlike
